options.content:
### Google Calendar Sync
Every activity a connected user logs is mirrored onto their Google Calendar. Writes are **best-effort** — Prog Strength stays the source of truth — so a failed write is recorded as resyncable state and a boot-time reconciler repairs it. That safety net is also the trap this dashboard watches for: **if the inline path breaks, the reconciler quietly covers for it and total volume looks fine**, which is why every panel splits `trigger=inline` from `trigger=reconcile`.

The healthy shape: syncs land inline within a second of logging, `reconcile` stays near zero, failures are zero, and **freshness stays well under the alert threshold**. `skipped` is normally the *largest* series and that is correct — it counts activities from users who never connected, plus anything logged before a user connected (the no-backfill cutoff).

Sections: **Sync health** (volume by result, the inline-vs-reconcile split, failures by type) · **Liveness & connections** (the durable freshness stamp the alert reads, and who is connected) · **Reconciler & backlog** (whether the repair pass is running, and whether it is keeping up).

Dashed yellow / red lines mark warning and critical levels. Hover any panel's title (ⓘ) for details and threshold meanings.

panels.title: Synced (24h)
panels.description: Activities successfully written to a Google Calendar in the last 24h, across both triggers. On a low-traffic install this is legitimately small — and legitimately zero on a day nobody trained. Zero is therefore NOT colored red here (that would cry wolf every rest day); the liveness question is answered by 'Time since last successful sync' below, which measures the gap rather than the count.

panels.title: Failed syncs (24h)
panels.description: Writes Google rejected in the last 24h. These are recorded as resyncable and retried by the reconciler, so a small number self-heals — but every one of them means a user's calendar was briefly wrong. Yellow at 1, red at 5. A sustained non-zero value with the count climbing means the retries are ALSO failing: check 'Failures by activity type' for whether it is one sport (a render bug) or all of them (Google, or the grant).

panels.title: Reconnects needed (24h)
panels.description: Syncs that failed because Google rejected the stored grant. The connection is flipped to `revoked` and the user is prompted to reconnect in the web app. One of these is a normal consequence of a user revoking access in their Google account settings; several across DIFFERENT users at once points at our OAuth client (a rotated secret, a changed consent scope), not at the users. Yellow at 1, red at 3.

panels.title: Time since last successful sync
panels.description:
Age of the newest successful write across CONNECTED users — the exact expression the dead-sync alert evaluates. Green under 48h, yellow past 48h, red past 72h (the alert's threshold).

This reads a DURABLE database stamp (user_calendar_connection.last_successful_sync_at), not a counter. That distinction is load-bearing: a per-process counter resets on every deploy, so `increase()` over it reports zero change no matter how healthy the integration is. The WHOOP dead-ingestion alert shipped exactly that mistake and fired continuously over working ingestion until migration 052 replaced it with a stamp like this one.

Shows an enormous value (and alerts) when nobody connected has ever synced — that is deliberate fail-loud behavior, not a bug. Empty when nobody is connected at all.

panels.title: Sync attempts by result
panels.description:
Every attempt, bucketed by outcome over 5-minute windows.

Read `skipped` as the baseline, not as a problem: it counts activities belonging to users with no calendar connection, plus anything logged before a user connected (the no-backfill cutoff). On a mostly-unconnected install it dominates, and that is correct behavior being reported honestly rather than hidden. `synced` should track actual training volume. `failed` and `reconnect_needed` should sit at zero. Dashed yellow / red lines mark the warning (1) and critical (5) levels used by the failed-sync alert.

panels.title: Inline vs reconciled writes
panels.description:
Successful writes split by what triggered them — THE panel for catching a silently-broken inline path.

Inline should carry essentially all of it: a user logs a session and the event appears within a second. `reconcile` is the boot-time repair pass, so a spike right after a deploy is normal (it is picking up anything missed while the API was down). What is NOT normal is reconcile carrying a steady share while inline sits flat — that means the request-path hooks stopped firing and the repair pass is papering over it. Total volume would look perfectly healthy; only this split exposes it. Dashed yellow / red mark 1 and 5 reconciled writes per window.

panels.title: Failures by activity type
panels.description: Failed and reconnect-needed writes broken down by sport. The breakdown is the diagnosis: failures confined to ONE activity type point at that type's calendar renderer (a manifest producing something Google rejects), while failures across ALL types at once point at the shared path — the Google API, the network, or the OAuth grant. Dashed yellow / red mark the warning (1) and critical (5) levels.

panels.title: Sync outcomes by activity type
panels.description: Successful writes by sport — the shape of what is actually reaching the calendar. Useful mainly as a sanity check against the app: if the user logged a hike this morning and `hiking` never appears here, the gap is between the hook and Google, not in the data. A type that NEVER appears despite being logged is the signal that its descriptor is not registered, or that its renderer is returning nothing.

panels.title: Time since last successful sync
panels.description:
The freshness gauge over time — this rule's alerting expression, plotted. It should saw-tooth: climbing steadily between sessions, dropping to near zero every time someone logs an activity. A line that climbs without ever dropping is a dead integration, and that is precisely what the critical alert fires on. Dashed yellow at 48h, red at 72h (the alert threshold).

A flat line at a very large value means nobody connected has ever synced — deliberately fail-loud rather than silently absent. The series is empty when nobody is connected at all, so an install nobody uses never pages.

panels.title: Connections by status
panels.description:
Calendar connections by lifecycle status, refreshed every 5 minutes from the database. `connected` is the population this whole dashboard is about, and it gates the liveness alert so an install nobody has connected never pages.

Watch for `connected` stepping DOWN while `revoked` steps up by the same amount: that is a grant going bad, and it is the user-visible symptom of the reconnect-needed counter above. A drop with no matching rise means someone disconnected outright, which deletes the row.

panels.title: Reconciler passes by result
panels.description:
One increment per reconciler pass, which runs once per API boot. On a stable deployment this is sparse by design — a flat zero line here just means nothing has restarted, not that anything is broken.

`error` means the pass could not even list what it owed (a database problem), so nothing was repaired that boot; the safety net was down. `cancelled` means shutdown interrupted a pass mid-flight, which is harmless — the next boot resumes. Dashed yellow / red mark the warning (1) and critical (3) levels for failed passes.

panels.title: Unwritten backlog after the last pass
panels.description:
Activities still owing a Google write when the last reconciler pass finished — non-zero only when the pass hit its per-boot cap (`[calendar_sync] reconcile_max_per_boot`, default 200).

The cap exists because each repair is a real Google API call, and an unbounded pass after a long outage could trip rate limits and take down the integration it is trying to fix. So a spike here right after an outage is the system working. What matters is the TREND: a backlog that stays pinned across successive boots means the cap is too low for the write rate and events are drifting further behind — raise `reconcile_max_per_boot`. Dashed yellow at 1 (the cap was hit at all) and red at 200 (a full page, so more is certainly behind it).
